claims.text: Wear performance of high-entropy-alloy protective coatings is governed by an interaction between coating microstructure and the operative wear mechanism.
Smaller coating grain size leads to improved wear resistance.
A more uniform phase distribution leads to improved wear resistance.
Grain size and phase distribution influence abrasive, adhesive, and fatigue wear mechanisms.
Jointly reducing grain size and making the phase distribution uniform will reduce wear rate by 20–30% relative to the specified baseline.
The experimental baseline is a coating with a grain size of 10–15 μm and a non-uniform phase distribution.
The hypothesis is expected to hold over a grain-size range of 1–20 μm.
The hypothesis is expected to hold over a phase-distribution-uniformity range of 0–100%.
The relationship among grain size, phase distribution, and wear mechanism may depend on coating composition.
The relationship among grain size, phase distribution, and wear mechanism may depend on wear conditions.
Failure to obtain at least a 15% lower wear rate for the smaller-grained, uniformly phase-distributed coating relative to baseline would falsify the hypothesis.

contradictions.description: The prediction requires a 20–30% wear-rate reduction, whereas the falsification rule accepts any reduction of at least 15%. Thus, an observation such as a 16% reduction would contradict the stated predicted range but would not falsify the hypothesis.
